questions.stem: Which sentence is appropriate for a cover letter?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies formal tone free of contractions and slang.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Cover letter writing directly aligns with B2 writing forms and purpose.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student recognizes formal tone indicators (no contractions, no slang).
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks informal language like 'didn't' is acceptable.

options.label: A
options.text: I didn't get the job before, but I'm really good at this.
options.feedbackWrong: This contains contractions ('didn't', 'I'm') and informal tone. Use formal, full forms like 'did not' and 'I am'.

options.label: B
options.text: I have developed strong communication skills through my volunteer work.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This sentence uses formal language, no contractions, and clearly states a skill.

options.label: C
options.text: I think this job is awesome and I want it so bad!
options.feedbackWrong: Use of 'awesome', 'so bad', and exclamation mark is informal. Avoid emotional language in cover letters.

options.label: D
options.text: I am writing to apply for the position of... wait, let me check the job title again.
options.feedbackWrong: Hesitating or speaking to the reader in a conversational way is not professional. Keep the tone direct and confident.

questions.stem: Which formatting choice is correct for a cover letter?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies standard cover letter formatting (margins, font, spacing, alignment).
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Formatting is part of the writing form for cover letters.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student remembers formatting rules: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman or Arial 10-12 pt, 1.1-1.5 line spacing, left-aligned.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks decorative fonts or wider margins are acceptable.

options.label: A
options.text: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman 11 pt, 1.5 line spacing, left-aligned.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This matches standard professional formatting.

options.label: B
options.text: 0.5-inch margins, Comic Sans 14 pt, 2.0 line spacing, right-aligned.
options.feedbackWrong: Comic Sans is not professional; margins too small; line spacing too wide; right alignment unusual.

options.label: C
options.text: 1-inch margins, Arial 9 pt, 1.0 line spacing, justified.
options.feedbackWrong: 9 pt is too small; 1.0 line spacing is cramped; justified alignment can cause uneven spacing.

options.label: D
options.text: 1.5-inch margins, Times New Roman 12 pt, 1.0 line spacing, center-aligned.
options.feedbackWrong: Margins too wide; center alignment is not standard for cover letters.

questions.stem: Which opening sentence best follows cover letter introduction rules?
questions.successCriteria: Student writes an introduction that states position and interest without repeating header or asking if still hiring.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Cover letter structure is part of writing form.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student avoids common intro mistakes: asking if still hiring, repeating header info.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks asking if position is still open shows interest, or that repeating name/address is necessary.

options.label: A
options.text: I am writing to express my strong interest in the Marketing Assistant position at ABC Corp, as advertised on LinkedIn.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This directly states the position, company, and source of the ad.

options.label: B
options.text: My name is John Smith and I live at 123 Main St. I am applying for a job at your company.
options.feedbackWrong: Repeating name and address from the header is unnecessary. Also lacks specific position.

options.label: C
options.text: Are you still hiring for the position? I saw the ad and I think I'd be perfect.
options.feedbackWrong: Never ask if still hiring; it shows lack of research. Also informal tone.

options.label: D
options.text: I am sending you my resume and cover letter for your consideration. I hope it's not too late to apply.
options.feedbackWrong: Too vague; does not mention the specific position or company. Also shows uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which body paragraph best demonstrates tailoring to a job requirement?
questions.successCriteria: Student selects a paragraph that connects specific skills/experience to job requirements with examples.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Tailoring content to audience and purpose is a key writing skill.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that body should align skills with job requirements and provide evidence.
questions.commonMisconception: Student writes generic statements without linking to the job or providing examples.

options.label: A
options.text: I am a hard worker and always give 100%. I'm sure I can learn the job quickly.
options.feedbackWrong: Too generic; no specific skills or examples linked to the job. Use concrete achievements.

options.label: B
options.text: As a social media coordinator for two years, I increased engagement by 40% through targeted campaigns. This experience aligns with your need for a marketing assistant who can manage online platforms.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This connects past experience to the job requirement and uses a specific example.

options.label: C
options.text: I have been looking for a job in marketing for a long time. Your company seems like a great place to work.
options.feedbackWrong: Focuses on personal desire, not on what the candidate offers. No alignment with job requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: I took a marketing course in college. I got an A in it. I think that qualifies me for this position.
options.feedbackWrong: Too brief and lacks connection to job requirements. A grade alone is not strong evidence.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate word count for a cover letter?
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Length is part of the writing form conventions.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student remembers the word limit.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks longer is better, or shorter is fine.

options.label: A
options.text: 100-200 words
options.feedbackWrong: Too short; cover letter needs enough detail. Aim for 200-400 words.

options.label: B
options.text: 200-400 words
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Cover letters should be 200-400 words, one page.

options.label: C
options.text: 400-600 words
options.feedbackWrong: Too long; employers prefer concise letters. Keep it to one page.

options.label: D
options.text: No limit, as long as it fits on one page.
options.feedbackWrong: Even if one page, word count should stay within 200-400. Long paragraphs may be cut.

questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that personal opinions and irrelevant details do not belong in a summary.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
questions.alignmentNote: Summary writing is explicitly mentioned in B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows to exclude personal opinions and irrelevant information.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks their own opinion adds value to the summary.

options.label: A
options.text: The article describes three main causes of urban heat islands.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a factual main idea, appropriate for a summary.

options.label: B
options.text: I believe the government should do more to reduce heat islands.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Personal opinion should not be included in a summary.

options.label: C
options.text: One solution mentioned is planting more trees in cities.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a supporting detail, appropriate as long as it's key.

options.label: D
options.text: The author interviewed researchers from three universities.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a detail from the article; it may be relevant if it supports the main idea.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected informal option on diagnostic question 1.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes informal language, contractions, or emotional punctuation are acceptable in a cover letter.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter is a formal business document. It must use professional, objective language. Avoid contractions (e.g., don't, didn't), slang, emotional punctuation (!, ..., —), and subjective words (e.g., stupid, awesome). Instead, use full forms (do not, did not) and a confident, neutral tone.
miniLesson.example:
Informal: 'I didn't get the job before, but I'm really good at this.'
Formal: 'Although I have not held this exact role, I have developed strong skills through related experience.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a cover letter as a suit and tie, not a T-shirt and jeans. Always dress your language professionally.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which sentence is appropriate for a cover letter?
A) I didn't have much experience, but I'm a fast learner.
B) I bring a strong work ethic and adaptability to every role.
C) This job is totally awesome and I want it so bad!
guidedPractice.answer: B) I bring a strong work ethic and adaptability to every role.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following informal sentence to be formal and professional for a cover letter: 'I don't think I'm the best candidate, but I'll try my hardest.'
guidedPractice.answer: I am confident that my skills and dedication make me a strong candidate for this position.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one formal sentence for the body of a cover letter that highlights a skill without using any contractions, slang, or emotional punctuation. Use the skill 'communication'.
guidedPractice.answer: I have developed exceptional communication skills through leading team projects and presenting to diverse audiences.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected incorrect formatting option in diagnostic.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student may believe decorative fonts or wider margins are acceptable.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter must follow standard professional formatting: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman or Arial font at 10-12 pt, line spacing 1.1-1.5, double space between paragraphs, left-aligned. Consistent font throughout.
miniLesson.example: Correct: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman 11 pt, 1.5 line spacing, left-aligned. Incorrect: 0.5-inch margins, Comic Sans 14 pt, 2.0 line spacing, right-aligned.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 1 inch margins, 11 pt Times New Roman, 1.15 spacing, left-aligned – like a formal business letter.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which set of formatting rules is correct for a cover letter? A) 1-inch margins, Arial 10 pt, 1.1 line spacing, left-aligned. B) 1.5-inch margins, Times New Roman 12 pt, 2.0 line spacing, center-aligned. C) 0.75-inch margins, Calibri 11 pt, 1.5 line spacing, right-aligned.
guidedPractice.answer: A

guidedPractice.prompt: The following cover letter has formatting errors: '0.5-inch margins, Comic Sans 14 pt, 2.0 line spacing, center-aligned.' List three specific errors and suggest corrections.
guidedPractice.answer: Errors: margins should be 1 inch (not 0.5), font should be Times New Roman or Arial (not Comic Sans), size should be 10-12 pt (not 14), line spacing 1.1-1.5 (not 2.0), alignment left (not center).

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this header with correct formatting: 'Name: John Smith / Address: 123 Main St / Font: Arial 9 pt / Margins: 0.5 inch / Spacing: double'
guidedPractice.answer: Use 1-inch margins, Arial 11 pt, 1.15 line spacing, left-aligned. Header: John Smith, 123 Main St, etc. (format as required).

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly chooses an introduction that asks if still hiring or repeats header information.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that asking if the position is still open demonstrates interest, or that restating their name and address in the introduction is necessary.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter introduction should clearly state the specific position and company you are applying to, and express your interest. Do not ask if the company is still hiring (it suggests you haven't researched) and do not repeat information already in your header (your name, address, etc.).
miniLesson.example: Correct: 'I am writing to apply for the Marketing Assistant position at ABC Corp, as advertised on LinkedIn.' Incorrect: 'My name is John Smith, I live at 123 Main St. Are you still hiring for the position?'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Start with position and interest, not a question or repeat.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is an appropriate cover letter introduction? A) 'Are you still hiring for the receptionist job?' B) 'I am eager to apply for the receptionist position at your company.'
guidedPractice.answer: B) 'I am eager to apply for the receptionist position at your company.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this introduction to follow the rules: 'My name is Jane Doe. I am applying for a job at your company. Is the position still open?'
guidedPractice.answer: I am writing to express my interest in the [specific position] at [company name].

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a complete introduction sentence for a cover letter for a Graphic Designer position at DesignStudio. Include the position and company, and express interest.
guidedPractice.answer: I am writing to apply for the Graphic Designer position at DesignStudio, as I am very interested in contributing to your creative team.

reteachModules.trigger: The student's cover letter body fails to align skills with job requirements.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student does not understand that the body of a cover letter must directly connect their skills and experiences to the specific requirements of the job, using concrete examples.

miniLesson.explain: The body of your cover letter should show how your skills and experience match what the employer is looking for. Instead of listing everything you've done, choose key experiences that directly relate to the job description. Use specific examples and describe contributions you made. This demonstrates that you are a good fit.
miniLesson.example: For a marketing assistant position requiring social media management, you could write: 'In my previous role as social media coordinator, I managed Instagram and Facebook accounts, increasing engagement by 40% through targeted campaigns. This experience directly prepares me to handle your company’s online platforms.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Match your skills to the job like puzzle pieces. Each piece of experience should fit into a requirement in the job posting.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the job requirement and the candidate statement. Choose the option that best aligns the candidate's experience with the requirement. Requirement: 'Must have customer service experience.' Candidate Statement 1: 'I have worked in retail for five years, helping customers find products and resolving complaints.' Candidate Statement 2: 'I am good with people and like helping others.' Which statement is better tailored? Answer the letter.
guidedPractice.answer: Statement 1, because it gives specific context (retail) and actions (helping find products, resolving complaints) that match the requirement.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a sentence that tailors the following experience to the job requirement. Experience: You were president of the student council, organizing events and leading meetings. Job Requirement: The position requires strong leadership and project management skills. Write one sentence connecting your experience to the requirement.
guidedPractice.answer: As student council president, I led a team to organize school-wide events, demonstrating the leadership and project management skills required for this role.

guidedPractice.prompt: Evaluate the following body paragraph from a cover letter. Identify two ways it fails to tailor to the job requirement and rewrite it to be more effective. Requirement: The job needs someone with attention to detail and experience with data entry. Paragraph: 'I am a hard worker and I learn quickly. I have done many different jobs. I think I would be good at this job.'
guidedPractice.answer: The paragraph is too generic: it lacks specific mention of data entry and attention to detail. Rewrite: 'In my previous role as an administrative assistant, I was responsible for entering and verifying customer data, ensuring accuracy in over 500 records per week. This experience has honed my attention to detail and data entry speed, making me a strong fit for this position.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect word count for cover letter on diagnostic question Q5 (diag-olc4o-07-29-q5).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student believes cover letters can be shorter than 200 words or longer than 400 words, or that there is no length limit.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter must be 200–400 words and fit on one page. This ensures it is concise yet provides enough detail to showcase your qualifications. Employers expect a focused letter; too short may lack substance, too long may lose their interest.
miniLesson.example: Too short (150 words): 'I am applying for the job. I have skills. Please hire me.' Too long (500 words): A detailed essay describing every job duty from the past 10 years. Correct length (300 words): A well-structured letter with introduction, 2 body paragraphs connecting skills to the job, and a conclusion.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: 200-400 words, one page – like a tweet that's just a little longer.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the acceptable word count range for a cover letter? Choose the correct answer from: A) 100-200 words, B) 200-400 words, C) 400-600 words, D) No limit.
guidedPractice.answer: B) 200-400 words

guidedPractice.prompt: A student wrote 450 words for their cover letter. The letter has three body paragraphs. Which paragraph could be cut to reduce the word count to under 400 words? The paragraphs: (1) Introduction and interest, (2) Relevant experience with example, (3) Another job from 5 years ago with less relevance. Provide a revised version.
guidedPractice.answer: Cut paragraph 3. Revised: remove the third paragraph, keep intro and main experience paragraph. Result: ~350 words.

guidedPractice.prompt: Evaluate this cover letter excerpt: 'I am writing to apply for the sales associate position. I have experience in retail. I am a hard worker. I am available evenings. I think I would be great.' The total letter is 180 words. What is the main issue regarding length? How would you improve it?
guidedPractice.answer: The letter is too short (180 words). To improve: add specific examples of sales achievements, quantify results, explain how skills match the job. Aim for at least 200 words with concrete details.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q6 in diagnostic (err-summary-irrelevant).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student includes personal opinions or irrelevant details in a summary, not understanding that summaries should only contain main ideas and key supporting details from the source text without adding personal views or extraneous information.

miniLesson.explain: A summary is a concise restatement of the main ideas and key supporting details from a source text. It must be objective and free of personal opinions, judgments, or irrelevant information. Your summary should only include what the author wrote, not your own beliefs or additional facts not in the original. The maximum length is 250 words.
miniLesson.example:
Original text: 'The study found that urban heat islands increase temperatures by 3-5°C. Solutions include green roofs and reflective pavements.'
Inappropriate summary: 'The study found that urban heat islands increase temperatures, and I think the government should invest in solutions.'
Appropriate summary: 'The study reports that urban heat islands raise temperatures by 3-5°C and suggests green roofs and reflective pavements as solutions.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Stick to the facts, not your feelings. If it's not in the source, don't include it.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following sentences would be appropriate to include in a summary of an article?
A. 'The article explains three causes of climate change.'
B. 'I believe the article is well-written.'
C. 'The author mentioned that carbon emissions are a major factor.'
guidedPractice.answer: A and C are appropriate; B is a personal opinion.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Read this short passage: 'The new policy aims to reduce plastic waste by banning single-use plastics. Businesses must find alternatives within two years. Many environmental groups support the move.'
Which of the following is the best summary sentence?
A. 'The new policy bans single-use plastics, and businesses have two years to find alternatives, with environmental support.'
B. 'I think the new policy is great because it will reduce plastic waste.'
C. 'The policy is about plastics and businesses.'
guidedPractice.answer: A

guidedPractice.prompt:
Read this passage: 'According to the report, reading for 30 minutes daily improves vocabulary and concentration. Children who read regularly perform better in school.'
Write one sentence summary without adding personal opinion.
guidedPractice.answer: The report states that daily reading of 30 minutes enhances vocabulary and concentration, and that children who read regularly perform better in school.

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student believes longer summaries are more thorough or forgets the 250-word limit.

miniLesson.explain: Summaries must be concise and capture only the main idea and key supporting details from the source. The maximum word count is 250 words. Exceeding this limit shows poor selection of information and may include unnecessary details.
miniLesson.example:
Original summary (300 words): 'The article discusses climate change, its causes like greenhouse gases, effects like rising temperatures, and solutions such as renewable energy. It also mentions the Paris Agreement, which many countries signed. The author argues that immediate action is needed. In conclusion, climate change is a serious issue that requires global cooperation...'  

Revised summary (248 words): 'The article discusses climate change, its causes (greenhouse gases), effects (rising temperatures), and solutions (renewable energy). It highlights the Paris Agreement and stresses the need for immediate global action.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: 250 is the max—be concise and pack it in.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following summaries is within the 250-word limit? A) 245 words, B) 260 words, C) 250 words exactly.
guidedPractice.answer: Both A and C are within the limit (245 words and 250 words exactly are acceptable). B is 260 words and exceeds the limit.

guidedPractice.prompt: Below is a 300-word summary. Revise it to be under 250 words while keeping the main idea and key supporting details. Original: 'The article explains that deforestation is a major cause of biodiversity loss. It describes how cutting down forests destroys habitats for many species. The author also points out that deforestation contributes to climate change by releasing carbon dioxide. Solutions mentioned include sustainable logging and reforestation. The article concludes by urging governments to enforce stricter laws. In my opinion, these measures are essential.'
guidedPractice.answer: Revised: 'The article explains that deforestation causes biodiversity loss by destroying habitats and contributes to climate change by releasing carbon dioxide. Solutions include sustainable logging and reforestation, and the author urges governments to enforce stricter laws.' (Word count: ~50 words)

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a summary of the following article in no more than 250 words. Article: 'Researchers have found that regular exercise improves mental health by reducing anxiety and depression. The study followed 1,000 adults over five years and found that those who exercised three times per week reported 30% fewer symptoms. Exercise also boosts self-esteem and cognitive function. The authors recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week.'
guidedPractice.answer: A study of 1,000 adults over five years found that regular exercise (three times per week) reduces anxiety and depression symptoms by 30%. Exercise also improves self-esteem and cognitive function. The authors recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week for mental health benefits.

questions.stem: Which sentence is appropriate for the conclusion of a cover letter?
options: Thanks for your time—I'm super excited to hear from you!
I appreciate your consideration and look forward to the possibility of discussing my application further.
Hope you pick me! Let me know.
I didn't think I'd apply, but here I am.

questions.stem: Rewrite the following sentence to make it appropriate for a formal cover letter: 'I'm sure you guys will love my awesome resume.'
questions.rubric: Sentence is formal, no contractions (use 'I am'), no slang ('guys', 'awesome'), and no emotional punctuation. Accepts: 'I am confident that my resume will demonstrate my qualifications for this position.' or similar.

questions.stem: Which set of formatting rules is correct for a cover letter?
options: 1-inch margins, Arial 10 pt, 1.1 line spacing, left-aligned
1.5-inch margins, Times New Roman 12 pt, 2.0 line spacing, center-aligned
0.75-inch margins, Calibri 11 pt, 1.5 line spacing, right-aligned

questions.stem: A student submits a cover letter with 0.5-inch margins, Comic Sans 14 pt, 2.0 line spacing, and center alignment. Identify three specific formatting errors and provide the correct requirement for each.
questions.rubric: Must identify at least three of: margins should be 1 inch, font should be Times New Roman or Arial, size should be 10-12 pt, line spacing should be 1.1-1.5, alignment should be left.

retestCards.passRule: Answer q1 correctly and identify at least three errors correctly in q2.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate opening sentence for a cover letter introduction?
options: Are you still hiring for the marketing position?
My name is John Smith, and I am applying for the marketing position at your company.
I am writing to apply for the Marketing Coordinator role at XYZ Inc., as advertised on your website.
I have attached my resume for your consideration.

questions.stem:
Rewrite the following poor cover letter introduction so that it follows proper conventions:

'My name is Jane Doe. I am applying for a job at your company. Is the position still available?'
questions.rubric: The rewritten introduction must: (1) state the specific position and company name, (2) express interest in the role, (3) avoid asking if the position is still open, (4) avoid repeating personal information like name or address. Example: 'I am writing to apply for the [specific position] at [company name], as I am very interested in contributing to your team.'

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct multiple choice answer (index 2) AND the open-ended response must include a specific position and company, express interest, and avoid asking about hiring or repeating header info.

questions.stem:
Job posting: 'Must have proven ability to work under pressure and meet deadlines.' 
Which applicant statement best tailors their experience to this requirement?
options: I am very organized and always finish my work on time.
As a newspaper editor, I consistently met daily publication deadlines by coordinating with reporters under tight schedules.
I work well under pressure because I stay calm.

questions.stem: You have experience as a volunteer coordinator for a food bank, where you scheduled shifts, trained volunteers, and managed inventory. The job requires 'strong organizational and team management skills.' Write one sentence for your cover letter body that directly connects your experience to this requirement, using specific details.
questions.rubric: The sentence must mention specific responsibilities (e.g., scheduling, training, inventory) and explicitly link them to organizational or team management skills. Avoid generic statements.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must be answered correctly (index 1). Q2 must include at least one specific detail from the experience and a clear connection to the job requirement.

questions.stem: A classmate says cover letters can be written in 150 words or up to 500 words as long as they are interesting. Based on the lesson, which statement best corrects their understanding?
options: Cover letters have no strict word count, but should be concise.
Cover letters must be exactly 300 words, no more and no less.
Cover letters should be 200–400 words and fit on one page.
Cover letters can be up to 500 words if the applicant has a lot of experience.

questions.stem: A student's cover letter contains only 180 words. The letter says: 'I want the job. I am good at customer service. Please call me.' Identify the main problem related to the cover letter length requirement and explain one specific way to fix it so the letter meets the expected word range.
questions.rubric: Identifies that the letter is too short (below 200 words). Suggests one concrete way to expand, such as adding a specific example of customer service achievement, describing relevant experience in more detail, or including a second body paragraph. Response must mention 200–400 word range.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions answered correctly. Single-choice answer must be index 2. Open-ended must identify length issue (below 200 words) and suggest a specific expansion method.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage:
"A new study shows that students who eat breakfast score 10% higher on math tests. Researchers surveyed 500 students over one year and found a clear link between morning meals and academic performance."

Which of the following would be an appropriate sentence to include in a summary of this passage?
options: The study shows a link between breakfast and math scores.
I think every student should eat breakfast to do better in school.
The researchers surveyed 500 students, but the study might be flawed.

questions.stem:
Write a one-sentence summary of the following passage that includes only the main idea and key supporting details. Do not add personal opinions or irrelevant information.

Passage: "According to a recent report, urban gardens can reduce local temperatures by up to 2°C. They also provide fresh produce for communities. The report recommends that cities invest more in green spaces."
questions.rubric: The summary must include only facts from the passage: urban gardens reduce temperatures by up to 2°C, provide fresh produce, and the report recommends cities invest in green spaces. No personal opinions (e.g., 'I think this is a good idea') or irrelevant details (e.g., mentioning other benefits not in the passage). Conciseness is preferred.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly. For Q2, the answer must contain no personal opinions or irrelevant information beyond the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the summary word limit is correct?
options: Summaries must be exactly 250 words.
Summaries can be up to 250 words, including 250 words exactly.
Summaries must be under 250 words, with 250 being too many.
Summaries can be any length as long as they are concise.

questions.stem: Revise the following 300-word summary to be under 250 words while keeping the main idea and key supporting details. Original: 'The article explains that deforestation is a major cause of biodiversity loss. It describes how cutting down forests destroys habitats for many species. The author also points out that deforestation contributes to climate change by releasing carbon dioxide. Solutions mentioned include sustainable logging and reforestation. The article concludes by urging governments to enforce stricter laws. In my opinion, these measures are essential.'
questions.rubric: Answer must be 249 words or fewer, contain the main idea (deforestation causes biodiversity loss and climate change), include key supporting details (habitat destruction, CO2 release, solutions: sustainable logging/reforestation, call for stricter laws), and omit personal opinions ('In my opinion').

retestCards.passRule: Single choice must be correct; open-ended answer must meet rubric criteria (word count ≤249, includes main idea and key details, no personal opinion).

teacherEscalation.condition: student fails the same retest twice or scores in the lowest tier on two consecutive lesson diagnostics
teacherEscalation.message: 该学生需要人工短辅导；问题不是单题错误，而是核心概念系统没有建立。

dashboardFormat.objective: A cover letter is a non-fiction narrative text sent with a resume to a potential employer, highlighting skills, experience, and personal qualities relevant to the job.；Cover letter length is 200-400 words, single page.；Cover letter tone: formal, professional; avoid slang, contractions (don't, didn't), emotional punctuation (exclamation, ellipsis, dash), and subjective words like 'stupid'.

learningGoals.statement: Write a formal cover letter with appropriate tone, format, and structure for a job application.
Produce a concise summary that captures main ideas without personal opinion or irrelevant details.

cards.question: Which sentence is appropriate for a cover letter?
options: I didn't get the job before, but I'm really good at this.
I have developed strong communication skills through my volunteer work.
I think this job is awesome and I want it so bad!
I am writing to apply for the position of... wait, let me check the job title again.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student recognizes formal tone indicators (no contractions, no slang).
misconceptions: This contains contractions ('didn't', 'I'm') and informal tone. Use formal, full forms like 'did not' and 'I am'.
✓ Correct. This sentence uses formal language, no contractions, and clearly states a skill.
Use of 'awesome', 'so bad', and exclamation mark is informal. Avoid emotional language in cover letters.
Hesitating or speaking to the reader in a conversational way is not professional. Keep the tone direct and confident.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies formal tone free of contractions and slang.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Cover letter writing directly aligns with B2 writing forms and purpose.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks informal language like 'didn't' is acceptable.

cards.question: Which formatting choice is correct for a cover letter?
options: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman 11 pt, 1.5 line spacing, left-aligned.
0.5-inch margins, Comic Sans 14 pt, 2.0 line spacing, right-aligned.
1-inch margins, Arial 9 pt, 1.0 line spacing, justified.
1.5-inch margins, Times New Roman 12 pt, 1.0 line spacing, center-aligned.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student remembers formatting rules: 1-inch margins, Times New Roman or Arial 10-12 pt, 1.1-1.5 line spacing, left-aligned.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. This matches standard professional formatting.
Comic Sans is not professional; margins too small; line spacing too wide; right alignment unusual.
9 pt is too small; 1.0 line spacing is cramped; justified alignment can cause uneven spacing.
Margins too wide; center alignment is not standard for cover letters.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies standard cover letter formatting (margins, font, spacing, alignment).
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Formatting is part of the writing form for cover letters.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks decorative fonts or wider margins are acceptable.

cards.question: Which opening sentence best follows cover letter introduction rules?
options: I am writing to express my strong interest in the Marketing Assistant position at ABC Corp, as advertised on LinkedIn.
My name is John Smith and I live at 123 Main St. I am applying for a job at your company.
Are you still hiring for the position? I saw the ad and I think I'd be perfect.
I am sending you my resume and cover letter for your consideration. I hope it's not too late to apply.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student avoids common intro mistakes: asking if still hiring, repeating header info.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. This directly states the position, company, and source of the ad.
Repeating name and address from the header is unnecessary. Also lacks specific position.
Never ask if still hiring; it shows lack of research. Also informal tone.
Too vague; does not mention the specific position or company. Also shows uncertainty.
cards.successCriteria: Student writes an introduction that states position and interest without repeating header or asking if still hiring.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Cover letter structure is part of writing form.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks asking if position is still open shows interest, or that repeating name/address is necessary.

cards.question: Which body paragraph best demonstrates tailoring to a job requirement?
options: I am a hard worker and always give 100%. I'm sure I can learn the job quickly.
As a social media coordinator for two years, I increased engagement by 40% through targeted campaigns. This experience aligns with your need for a marketing assistant who can manage online platforms.
I have been looking for a job in marketing for a long time. Your company seems like a great place to work.
I took a marketing course in college. I got an A in it. I think that qualifies me for this position.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that body should align skills with job requirements and provide evidence.
misconceptions: Too generic; no specific skills or examples linked to the job. Use concrete achievements.
✓ Correct. This connects past experience to the job requirement and uses a specific example.
Focuses on personal desire, not on what the candidate offers. No alignment with job requirements.
Too brief and lacks connection to job requirements. A grade alone is not strong evidence.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects a paragraph that connects specific skills/experience to job requirements with examples.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Tailoring content to audience and purpose is a key writing skill.
cards.commonMisconception: Student writes generic statements without linking to the job or providing examples.

cards.question: What is the appropriate word count for a cover letter?
options: 100-200 words
200-400 words
400-600 words
No limit, as long as it fits on one page.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student remembers the word limit.
misconceptions: Too short; cover letter needs enough detail. Aim for 200-400 words.
✓ Correct. Cover letters should be 200-400 words, one page.
Too long; employers prefer concise letters. Keep it to one page.
Even if one page, word count should stay within 200-400. Long paragraphs may be cut.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Length is part of the writing form conventions.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks longer is better, or shorter is fine.

cards.question: Which sentence would be inappropriate to include in a summary of an article?
options: The article describes three main causes of urban heat islands.
I believe the government should do more to reduce heat islands.
One solution mentioned is planting more trees in cities.
The author interviewed researchers from three universities.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows to exclude personal opinions and irrelevant information.
misconceptions: This is a factual main idea, appropriate for a summary.
✓ Correct. Personal opinion should not be included in a summary.
This is a supporting detail, appropriate as long as it's key.
This is a detail from the article; it may be relevant if it supports the main idea.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that personal opinions and irrelevant details do not belong in a summary.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Summary writing is explicitly mentioned in B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks their own opinion adds value to the summary.

cards.question: What is the maximum word count for a summary in this course?
options: 150 words
250 words
300 words
No word limit
cards.diagnosis: Check if student remembers the 250-word maximum.
misconceptions: Too restrictive; the limit is 250 words.
✓ Correct. Summaries must be 250 words or fewer.
Too long; the limit is 250 words.
There is a 250-word limit to ensure conciseness.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Word limit is part of writing conventions for summaries.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks longer summaries are better or forgets the limit.
